paragraphs.heading: Cooling after an eruption
paragraphs.text: A volcanic winter is a drop in global temperatures that follows a large, sulfur-rich, particularly explosive volcanic eruption. Droplets of sulfuric acid obscure the Sun and raise Earth's albedo, which means more solar radiation is reflected. Tree-ring temperature reconstructions, historical records of dust veils and ice core studies have confirmed that massive volcanic injections of SO₂ directly caused some of the coldest years of the last five millennia.

paragraphs.heading: Gas, not ash
paragraphs.text: An explosive eruption releases magma materials into the atmosphere as volcanic ash and gases. Most of the ash settles to the ground within a few weeks and affects only the local area for a short time. The climate effects depend mainly on how much SO₂ and H₂S is injected into the stratosphere. There, on a timescale of a week, these gases react with OH and H₂O and form H₂SO₄, and the H₂SO₄ aerosols that result produce the dominant radiative effect. The aerosols cool the surface by reflecting solar radiation, and they warm the stratosphere by absorbing terrestrial radiation.

paragraphs.heading: How long the haze lasts
paragraphs.text: The aerosols can circle the hemisphere of the eruption in a matter of weeks. They persist with a decay time of about a year, so their radiative impact can last for several years. Injection height matters. If the SO₂ stays confined to the troposphere, the resulting aerosols remain for only a few days, because precipitation removes them efficiently. The season of the eruption and the latitude of the volcano also strongly influence how the volcanic cloud spreads in the stratosphere and how it affects climate.

paragraphs.heading: Size does not predict the cold
paragraphs.text: Surface temperature observations after historic eruptions show no correlation between the size of an eruption, as represented by the VEI or the eruption volume, and how severe the cooling was. The reason given is that the amount of SO₂ emitted does not correlate with eruption size.

paragraphs.heading: Signs in the sky
paragraphs.text: The sulfate aerosol interacts strongly with solar radiation by scattering it, and this produces striking optical effects in the stratosphere. Among them are dimming of the Sun, coronae or Bishop's rings, peculiar colors at twilight, and dark total lunar eclipses. Historical records of such events are indications of volcanic winters, and they date back to before the Common Era.

paragraphs.heading: When the cold outlasts the aerosols
paragraphs.text: It has been proposed that the cooling from eruptions can extend beyond the first several years, lasting for decades and possibly even millennia. The hypothesis rests on positive feedback mechanisms involving ice and ocean. In the first few years the aerosols can cause significant cooling, which can lower the snowline widely and allow sea ice, ice caps and continental glaciers to expand rapidly. Ocean temperatures then fall and surface albedo rises, which reinforces the expansion further. This loop allows the cooling trend to persist for centuries or longer, even after the aerosols have dissipated.

paragraphs.heading: The Toba debate
paragraphs.text: One eruption whose climate effects are vigorously debated is that of the Youngest Toba Tuff from Toba Caldera, 74,000 years ago. It is regarded as the largest known Quaternary eruption, with a magma volume two orders of magnitude greater than that of Tambora, the largest historical eruption. Sulfate measurements from polar ice cores of about that age point to four atmospheric aerosol events that could potentially be put down to it. For these four events, the calculated loading of sulfate in the stratosphere ranges from 219 to 535 million tonnes. That is 1 to 3 times greater than the loading from the Samalas eruption of 1257 CE.
